title: Building a personal verification routine
body_md:
## A routine you can use while stressed

Social-engineering awareness is useful only if it changes what you do. Use a short routine for any unexpected request that would move money, expose a code or document, install software, grant access or change a trusted contact. It need not prove the inbound message false. Its purpose is to make the **next action** depend on a source the requester does not control.

**1. Stop the inbound action.** Do not click, transfer, read a code or approve a new recipient while the person is guiding you. You may note the claimed organization, issue and deadline without giving sensitive information. End the call or conversation politely. If immediate physical danger is described, use the local emergency number you already know; a safety emergency deserves a real response, not an online checklist.

**2. Select a trusted route.** Open an app from your own device, use a saved contact, the number on a card or statement, a workplace directory, or a portal you already use. Do not use the contact details inside the message or the displayed caller ID. A search result can also be an advert or imitation, so prefer established records. For a family claim, call the person on your saved number or ask another trusted relative if you cannot reach them.

**3. Restate the exact request.** Ask the independent contact: “Did you ask me to change this account, send this payment, or provide this code? What is the normal process?” Confirm both the underlying problem and the proposed remedy. An official channel may show that a real issue exists but that the inbound remedy was invented.

**4. Decide and document.** If verified, complete the action only through the institution’s ordinary workflow. If unconfirmed, pause; do not let the original deadline force a workaround. If you already acted, contact the account, bank or payment provider promptly through its verified support channel. The options depend on what was exposed and on local law; there is no guaranteed reversal. Save relevant records privately.

Make the routine a household or team agreement. “We verify changes of payment details through a second known route” lets everyone follow the same rule without accusing a caller or feeling rude. Rehearse with the synthetic exercise below, then adapt the route list to your actual services without writing any real numbers or secrets into this lesson.

widget_config.goal: Run a repeatable four-part verification routine before acting on an unexpected high-stakes request.
widget_config.today_action: Write a private, offline list of two established contact routes and tell one trusted person that you will use it for unexpected payment or access requests.
widget_config.scope: General routine based on UK NCSC and US FTC consumer guidance. Emergency, provider-response and reporting procedures are local; do not enter real contact details in the lesson.

sources.title: UK NCSC — how to spot a scam message or call
sources.scope: UK public guidance, published 2021, reviewed 2022; cues and independent contact, not a diagnostic test.

sources.title: US FTC — unexpected calls about money at risk
sources.scope: US consumer alert (January 2026); call back using an existing card, statement, app or official site.

sources.title: US FTC — fake family emergencies
sources.scope: US consumer guidance (2023); voice cloning, secrecy and direct contact with family.

sources.title: US FTC — How to Avoid a Scam
sources.scope: US consumer guidance (2023); impersonation, pressure, payment methods and independent contact.

blocks.title: Synthetic: family emergency with a familiar voice
blocks.situation: A caller sounds like your brother, says he is stranded, and asks you to buy gift cards immediately without telling anyone.
blocks.analysis: The voice, secrecy and payment method create a serious warning. FTC guidance notes voice imitation is possible. End the call and use the number already saved for your brother; if unreachable, contact another relative. If danger is credible, use relevant local emergency services. Do not use gift-card codes as an emergency channel.

blocks.title: Synthetic: verified repair visit
blocks.situation: Your building management app, which you opened independently, shows a repair booked for tomorrow. A technician at the door refers to the matching work order; the management desk confirms their identity through the number on your lease.
blocks.analysis: A surprise in-person request can be legitimate. Independent work-order and desk confirmation allow the visit under building rules. Still do not share account passwords or unrelated documents. A verification routine can end in a justified yes.

blocks.title: The water-leak request
blocks.setup: A fictional message claiming to be from building management says: ‘There may be a water leak in Unit 204, next to yours. Send your door code to our technician right away so we can check your apartment.’ The first two decisions test how to pause and choose a contact route. The third is a separate leak report that you check independently, regardless of those choices; the fourth is an explicit what-if after disclosure. No real address, access code or phone number is used.

steps.prompt: The message asks you to send your door code to a “technician” right away. What first?

choices.text: Send it; a leak may damage the building.
choices.consequence: You may give access to an unverified person.
choices.explanation: A real maintenance problem still deserves an independently verified access process.

choices.text: Pause the code request and note the claimed leak and unit without sending access data.
choices.consequence: You retain the issue to check while protecting the code.
choices.explanation: Stopping a credential transfer need not mean ignoring a possible leak.

steps.prompt: Which contact will verify the request?

choices.text: The management app or phone number on your existing lease.
choices.consequence: You contact the party through an established route.
choices.explanation: Ask whether there is an open work order and what access method is authorized.

choices.text: The callback number in the same message.
choices.consequence: The original sender controls the supposed check.
choices.explanation: Use a number or app you held before the message.

steps.prompt: Separate new leak report: you independently call the management desk using the number on your existing lease. The desk confirms a leak but says staff do not need residents’ door codes. A message nevertheless asks for yours. What do you do?

choices.text: Send the code because the leak is real.
choices.consequence: The real problem would be used to justify a false remedy.
choices.explanation: Verification must cover the requested action, not just the event.

choices.text: Follow the desk’s documented access arrangement and report the code request.
choices.consequence: You address the leak through an authorized process.
choices.explanation: This is the routine’s key distinction: real problem, unverified remedy.

steps.prompt: Suppose you had already shared the code. What is the next action?

choices.text: Tell the verified desk, change or disable the code through the authorized process, and keep the message privately.
choices.consequence: You respond to the exposure without using the suspicious sender.
choices.explanation: Steps depend on the building system; the desk can advise the actual procedure.

choices.text: Do nothing because the desk confirmed a leak.
choices.consequence: An exposed code may still allow unauthorized entry.
choices.explanation: Contact the verified management team about changing access and their incident process.

blocks.debrief: Debrief: the contact-route choice does not itself produce a real-desk finding. In the separate third snapshot, you make that independent call explicitly: the leak is real, but the code request is unauthorized. The final what-if tests recovery after disclosure. Replay the full stop → known route → exact request → response routine.

questions.prompt: A known friend’s account asks for a transfer to a new recipient. What is the best check?

choices.text: Use a previously saved separate route to confirm the specific transfer and recipient.
choices.explanation: Correct: a familiar account can be compromised, and recipient details need their own check.

choices.text: Reply in the same thread asking “Is this really you?”
choices.explanation: A compromised account can answer within that thread.

questions.prompt: A verified service confirms a real deadline but says the inbound link is not theirs. What follows?

choices.text: Use the service’s normal workflow for the real deadline.
choices.explanation: Correct: confirm both problem and remedy, then act through the trusted route.

choices.text: The deadline must be fake too, so ignore it.
choices.explanation: A real task can be attached to a false link.

questions.prompt: You already gave a code to an inbound caller. What is the priority?

choices.text: Wait to see whether anything happens.
choices.explanation: Delay can leave an account at risk.

choices.text: Use the account provider’s verified recovery and support route promptly.
choices.explanation: Correct: report what was exposed and follow provider-specific steps without trusting the caller.
